projectOutComesReport:
This project led to the development of chatbot driven technologies that can be integrated with programmable science gateways, data archives and cloud platforms in data-intensive application case studies. The project outcomes were made openly available, and disseminated through open-source repositories, as well as in conference/workshop venues that attract CI and SG communities from diverse disciplines. New customized data processing workflows were developed to address specific characteristics of the variety of data types relating to use cases in neuroscience, bioinformatics and health sciences. The resulting best practices from our customizations can be used in diffusion to other scientific applications (e.g., manufacturing, chemistry that benefit from social sciences) that benefit from guided interfaces and recommender-based systems to help researchers and educators handle big data processing needs. The technology prototypes from above investigations and experiments can also be used as plug-ins within emerging science gateway environments that leverage infrastructure environments (including NSG, XSEDE, CyVerse, JetStream, AWS), and were used as educational materials in curriculum for hands-on training of undergraduate and graduate students in regular courses and summer programs at MU and a Hispanic serving institution i.e., TTU.

 

The project made impacts to the discipline of Communication in two significant ways. First, this research extended the communication theory of diffusion by exploring how a chatbot (instead of a human agent) can assist human users in adopting and implementing an innovation (the KnowCOVID-19 Science Gateway in this case). Traditional diffusion research focuses on how human agents (e.g., opinion leaders, influencers) can assistant with user adoption and implementation. This research highlights the contribution of computer agents. Second, having the chatbot answer user queries represents a novel form of human-machine communication. This research specifically examined how a chatbot can engage in advice giving (in terms of how to use the gateway) to users, thus adding to the field of human-machine communication research.

abstractText:
The connections between students' home and family contexts and the activities of formal schooling are critical to support meaningful learning and family engagement in formal schooling. The need to better understand and make use of those connections is particularly important for multilingual learners whose family and cultural contexts may differ significantly from school contexts and their teachers' own experiences. The goal of this project is to develop and study a mathematics partnership that engages multilingual children, their teachers, and their parents in mathematical experiences together.  These mathematical experiences are designed to advance equity in mathematics education for multilingual students.  The project will design professional learning opportunities for parents, teachers, and students, and study the ways in which the professional learning opportunities influence teacher beliefs, quality of instruction, parent beliefs, and teacher and parent understanding of positioning.

This project uses a design-based implementation research (DBIR) approach, along with principles of Social Design Experiments to engage in iterative cycles of inquiry to develop, implement, and refine the model.  Parents, teachers, and students in three states (Arizona, Maryland, and Missouri) will be recruited that represent diverse populations both with respect to demographics and with respect to the policy contexts surrounding multilingual learners. Two cohorts of parents will be invited to participate in the parent-teacher study group, one consisting of 6 parents and teachers per site and one consisting of 20 parents and their children’s teachers per site. In each iteration, data will be collected at multiple time points related to teachers’ beliefs about effective math instruction for multilingual students; quality of mathematics instruction for linguistically diverse students; focus group interviews with parents and students, and video records of teachers and parents working with their students doing mathematics during study group convenings. Data analysis will blend quantitative and qualitative methods.  Quantitative methods will include t-tests, multivariate, and correlational analyses to examine changes in teacher beliefs, instructional quality, and the relationships between the two.  Qualitative analyses using thematic coding and discourse analysis will be used to analyze study group meetings and outcomes related to parent and teacher positioning of multilingual learners.

The Discovery Research preK-12 program (DRK-12) seeks to significantly enhance the learning and teaching of science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) by preK-12 students and teachers, through research and development of innovative resources, models and tools. Projects in the DRK-12 program build on fundamental research in STEM education and prior research and development efforts that provide theoretical and empirical justification for proposed projects.

projectOutComesReport:
The Together - Parents, Teachers, and Multilingual Children Doing Mathematics project (TOGETHER) developed and studied an innovative mathematical partnership that engaged teachers, parents, and multilingual children in grades 2-5, from schools in underserved communities. The partnership aimed to 1) establish collaborative relations between the school and the community 2) leverage the knowledge and expertise of children and families as a resource in teaching and learning mathematics with a focus on problem-solving; and 3) collaborate with teachers and parents to create environments that encourage the equitable participation of children in math learning. Across the five years of the project, we worked with 46+25 (71) teachers, 57 parents, and 65 children (in the workshops) across three geographically diverse regions in the country. Furthermore, through the teachers involved in the project, we reached out to 529 students in their classrooms (grades 2-5).

The research in TOGETHER expanded knowledge and theory related to how bringing parents and teachers together to explore and discuss mathematics can strengthen the mathematics learning opportunities for multilingual students. Specifically, our research shed light on pathways and barriers to creating mathematical partnerships from the perspectives of both teachers and parents. The barriers identified included limited opportunities for meaningful communication between parents and teachers, lack of integration of the mathematical knowledge of parents into the mathematics lessons, top-down curriculum mandates, and a school-centric model of parental engagement. On the other hand, creating spaces for mothers and teachers to interact and share experiences helped address these challenges through building mutual trust and recognizing parents as intellectual resources. Our research also shows the potential of having parents and teachers co-designing lessons for classroom implementation, as the different expertises of parents and teachers are brought together to provide learning opportunities that affirm the cultural and linguistic identities of multilingual students. Through opportunities for teachers and parents to explore mathematics together, teachers enhanced their understanding of the home everyday practices, which they could then bring into the classroom. On the other hand, parents developed a better understanding of what school mathematics teaching was like, which they could use to better support their children at home. Teacher professional development focused on connecting language supports with specific mathematical content resulted in broader and richer participation of multilingual learners in the classroom. Our findings on parents-children interactions on problem-solving tasks show a range of strategies that parents used to support their children, including using their home language and English, storytelling, and sharing of expertise. These findings can support teachers implementing problem-solving in their classrooms. All these experiences where teachers learn with and from parents can support their classroom teaching. Classroom observations pointed to the critical role of coordinating the language and mathematics teaching strategies for student participation.  

Research findings from TOGETHER have been disseminated through publications and presentations at conferences (local, national, and international). We have included teachers, and most notably, parents as co-presenters at several conferences. A list of project publications and presentations is available on our website.

Outcomes of the TOGETHER project include a set of 3 professional learning modules and 3 mathematics tasks. Each module contains a refined collection of activities (i.e., mathematics tasks, videos, collaborative group activities, reflection prompts, lesson analysis and design, etc.) for sessions with teachers and parents together, sessions with just teachers or just parents, or parents and children, and sessions that include teachers, parents, and children. The Introductory module contains activities to have families and teachers develop rapport and build community. It also is designed to begin to activate prior knowledge and build background related to the main module themes: Funds of Knowledge, and Language in relation to mathematics. The module on Funds of Knowledge contains activities to introduce the idea of funds of knowledge, and valuing family/community knowledge.  Participants are encouraged to think about the assets within communities, and the knowledge that the caregivers of students can bring to the mathematics education of their children. The module on language contains activities to support families and teachers to examine the role of language in mathematics lessons and reflect upon their own practices in supporting their children/students to develop language in the context of mathematics learning. We also include a list of key principles that informed the implementation and design of our mathematics partnership with teachers and parents; such principles can serve as a guide for the implementation of the modules in other contexts. We created video cases which are presentations that contain videos from workshops or panels, accompanied by facilitation guides, which can be used to facilitate discussion or analysis. We also created 4 digital stories that share the voice and perspective of participants about the project.  These modules, video cases and digital stories can be used for teacher professional learning, teacher preparation, and parent / family engagement initiatives. All the materials can be found in our project website: https://sites.google.com/umd.edu/togethermath/home

abstractText:
The broader impact/commercial potential of this I-Corps project is the development of software that will serve as an aid to the pathologist to provide more accurate diagnoses using histopathology images. The software will be deployed on the cloud so that it can be used anywhere, anytime through a web portal using a desktop, laptop, tablet, or a smart-phone. The software has the potential to dramatically speed up the disease diagnosis process with increased accuracy, which in turn will result in improved quality of care and better patient outcomes.

This I-Corps project is based on the development of novel deep learning techniques for whole-slide image analysis to aid pathologists in making a better diagnosis for diseases such as tuberculosis. Pathologists make a diagnosis based on recognizing patterns in histopathology images. Recognizing pathology patterns takes many years of training. After training, pathologists spend significant amount of time doing pattern recognition for the rest of their life. With the potential to save time and effort for pathologists, and inspired by the recent success of deep learning on natural images, there is a need to develop artificial intelligence models to recognize patterns in histopathology images. In addition to tuberculosis, the proposed techniques and software prototype could be extended to the diagnosis of other diseases in the future.

During this project period, we first went through a 6-weeks virtual cohort training camp, followed by many customer discovery activities. The cohort training camp is phenomenal and totally opened our vision and mind. We conducted many customer discovery activities during and after the cohort training camp to explore the commercial potential of the deep learning technology for digital pathology. We interviewed many pathologists and attended trade shows such as the Digital Pathology & AI world congress. All these activities have enabled us to obtain a much clearer picture of what to do next for our technology. During this project period we are also able to find some potential collaborations in commercializing the technology. Overall, we are very grateful to the support of NSF. The I-Corps experience is transformative for all the project members. Besides our initial research on AI-based TB diagnosis, we plan to develop some AI-enhanced tools for assisting pathologists for more challenging cases. This could be very beneficial to the society and definitely has market value. That will be our plan in the next phase of the project. We plan to keep working on the technology and in the meantime, we will be looking for additional funding support to enable us to continue developing the prototype product and seeking commercialization.

abstractText:
This RAPID project will compare epidemic patterns and Missouri residents’ responses in the 1918 influenza pandemic to those occurring at present during the COVID-19 pandemic, with primary attention paid to urban-rural differences. The research will increase understanding of how life situations in urban versus rural settings affect epidemic disease experiences and will provide knowledge of important community characteristics that put residents at greater risk during the current pandemic. The study will also shed light on which characteristics of a region have been stable over long periods of time and which are aspects of modern life and perhaps more malleable. The research is therefore time-sensitive because the investigators will expeditiously communicate project findings relevant to the current pandemic to the Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services. In addition, this project will provide student training in data collection and first-hand experience in conducting research to help deal with an unforeseen and serious public health event. 

A new coronavirus, SARS-CoV-2, to which humans possess little underlying immunity, has been spreading throughout the globe. In this pandemic setting, rural regions may face challenges that are not present in urban areas. As there is currently no vaccine, it is critical to devise effective strategies quickly, to protect rural regions from echo waves of the virus that may circulate over the next few years. The world experienced a similar situation in 1918-19 when a new, lethal strain of influenza began to infect humans. Although there are significant differences between these two pandemics, the viruses have similar modes of transmission and overall impacts on human communities. Understanding the experiences and responses of rural citizens to these two pandemics provides important insights that may lead to new public health strategies that are more tailored to the needs of rural residents during major disease outbreaks. The project involves in-depth comparative analysis of mortality and morbidity patterns during the 1918 influenza pandemic and the present COVID-19 pandemic in the state of Missouri. Analysis will focus on data aggregated at the county level and will determine county characteristics (e.g., population density, number of hospitals, household composition, proximity to large urban area, ethnic composition, mobility patterns) that are associated with death and/or illness rates during the two pandemics. Historical data from the Missouri 1918 influenza pandemic will be examined to identify control strategies used in different counties during the pandemic, determine their effectiveness, and assess whether they would be of use during the present pandemic. This in turn can aid in the development of potential strategies that public health authorities can add to the arsenal already being used in rural counties.

projectOutComesReport:
This project compared the 1918 influenza pandemic with the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic in the state of Missouri, focusing on differences between urban and rural populations and geographic regions. Specific research questions sought to address the timing and geographic patterns of spread for both pandemics, looking closely at rural-urban relationships and socioeconomic and cultural attributes of the population. To do this work, investigators collected the number of daily deaths by county during the 1918 influenza pandemic and both cases and deaths by day and county during the COVID-19 pandemic. In addition, socioeconomic and demographic data for all counties in the state of Missouri in the early 20th and early 21st centuries were collected. The socioeconomic and demographic data were used to separate the state?s counties into four distinct geographic regions during each of the two time periods, and in addition, a second classification divided the counties into three categories: rural, semi-rural and urban. Pandemic patterns were then examined using each of these two county classification schemes.

The major finding resulting from analyses of data from the 1918 influenza pandemic is the discovery of a large and late wave of flu deaths in Missouri in February of 1920. In the state as a whole, this wave was nearly as large as the main fall 1918 wave of the pandemic. Furthermore, in 25% of the state?s counties it was actually larger than the earlier wave. The influenza death data also indicate that flu mortality was greatest in urban populations over the three-year course of the pandemic. These findings contribute to the body of studies of the 1918 influenza pandemic worldwide and provide additional perspectives on how an epidemic disease resulting from a new pathogen transitions to an endemic disease.

Results from analyses of the COVID-19 data indicate differences in the disease?s impact on urban and rural populations across the course of the pandemic. Early in the pandemic, urban population centers experienced the highest rates of mortality and morbidity from COVID-19. This pattern shifted in late 2020, when rural populations in Missouri experienced higher rates of illness and death and rural counties have continued to be hit harder than urban populations since that time. This finding is important for understanding the disparate timing of COVID-19 impacts in rural and urban locations and will be of use when preparing for future disease outbreaks that have the potential for wide geographic spread.

Comparisons of the 1918 influenza pandemic and COVID-19 has allowed for a better understanding of the use of public health policy, like masking and quarantine orders, over time in the state. It also has demonstrated the continued impact of social determinants of health, such as education and socioeconomic status, on communities during a pandemic. Consistently, communities with lower socioeconomic status, lower access to health care, and lower rates of education experienced higher rates of illness and death during both pandemics in the state.

The broader impacts of this project extend well beyond the increased knowledge of the impact of the 1918 influenza and COVID-19 pandemics in Missouri. This project was able to support and train five graduate students in three academic fields (anthropology, statistics, and public health), as well as provide opportunities for undergraduate students pursuing a variety of majors to earn course credit or volunteer and gain research experience of relevance to today?s world. Both graduate and undergraduate students were trained in research methods in historical epidemiology, public health, and statistics, completed masters? theses or other formal reports, gained required internship credit, and presented posters and papers at local and national conferences. This project brought together senior researchers from several academic disciplines, including anthropology, statistics, mathematics, and medicine, thereby fostering interdisciplinary communication. Investigators also participated in activities that provided health care professionals with continuing education credits needed to maintain their licensure. Finally, investigators on this project participated in the national conversation during the pandemic by giving interviews to many local, regional, national, and international media outlets. During the uncertainty of the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic, their expertise in the 1918 flu was sought after by both health professionals and the general public.

abstractText:
The broader impact/commercial potential of this I-Corps project is pivoted around the emerging whole slide imaging market segment in digital pathology. The digital pathology market is predicted to reach over $800 million by 2025. The motivation of this project stems from the gigabyte size of whole slide images (WSIs), which are digital images of glass slides produced at near optical resolution. With rapid increase in the number of WSIs produced by hospitals and pathology labs, the storage and management of WSIs has become an urgent problem to tackle for next-generation image analytics. The commercial viability of the project can significantly impact researchers, medical professionals, software developers, and IT staff who wish to manage large number of WSIs using modern cluster computing and big data techniques. Thus, next-generation image analytics (e.g., using deep learning) for automatic detection and analysis of cellular and morphological features in human tissues can be performed faster on large numbers of WSIs. The potential societal benefit of the project includes enabling improved diagnosis of diseases by pathologists using next-generation image analytics and the creation of a tech startup leading to new jobs. This project will provide training to two Ph.D. students from underrepresented groups in STEM.

This I-Corps project is based on a software technology that aims to solve the fundamental problem of scalable storage of WSIs and fast retrieval of tiles using a commodity cluster and big data techniques. The value proposition of the technology is efficient and cost-effective storage of large-scale WSIs and fast retrieval of tiles to enable next-generation image analytics for human disease diagnosis. The technology encompasses intelligent data partitioning using space-filling curves, in-memory data structures, and effective organization of tiles to enable fast retrieval of tiles during image analysis. It employs space-efficient storage formats to maximize storage efficiency. On an average, it required a few seconds to retrieve a single tile on 80 WSIs using a 16-node cluster. Therefore, we believe next-generation image analytics on WSIs (e.g., using deep learning) can run faster on large number of WSIs, which can consume terabytes of storage, through faster access of image tiles. As the technology relies on commodity hardware and open source software, it is cost-effective and can be easily deployed as a product or a service. The technology has the potential to advance the state-of-the-art in WSI storage and management using a big data approach.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

projectOutComesReport:
The team had developed a technology that can store and manage large number of digital slides of human tissues. These slides are very large in size and hence require a big data approach to manage them. The team explored if their technology can be commercialized as digital pathology solutions are being adopted in clinical practice. 

Intellectual Merit:

- The team spoke to 110+ potential customers who directly or indirectly are impacted by the emerging market of digital pathology. The interviewees ranged from C-level executives, to clinicians, to residents and fellows, to sales and marketing people in the area of pathology. The team developed a business canvas model for the technology by clearly articulating the value propositions, customer segments, customer relations, revenue streams, and others. They learned that there was less commercial interest in storage and management of these digital slides today. However, there appears to be more interest in using AI for diagnostic purposes.

- The technology was further developed to improve its processing capability.

- The team went through a rigorous I-Corps training program and learned how to move technology from the lab to the marketplace.

 

Broader Impact:

- A total of three PhD students were trained; two of them were from underrepresented groups in STEM.

- The technology was presented at an international conference in 2020.
